claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA is single-phase BCC.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has high density.
The baseline alloy exhibits brittle room-temperature behavior with elongation below 1%.
Adding 2-5 at.% Al to Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will induce a secondary intermetallic phase.
The Al-induced secondary phase will be B2 or Laves.
Casting followed by heat treatment can promote transformation of an initially BCC refractory alloy into a two-phase microstructure.
The secondary phase will form a reticulated network at grain boundaries and within the BCC matrix.
A secondary intermetallic network will deflect and blunt cracks.
Crack deflection through tortuous paths will improve room-temperature ductility.
The secondary precipitates will be coherent or semi-coherent with the matrix.
Secondary-phase precipitates can impede dislocation mobility and produce precipitation-like hardening.
Al addition will produce room-temperature elongation to fracture above 5%.
Al addition will improve strength-ductility synergy while maintaining high strength.
Al addition will cause a moderate increase in alloy density.
Because Al is lighter than Hf, Mo, Ta, Zr, and Ti, its addition may slightly decrease density or leave it comparable to the baseline.
The intervention is effective only within an Al-content range that produces a continuous network without large brittle clusters.
Excessive Al may generate brittle intermetallic structures and reduce ductility.
A 0, 2, 5, and 10 at.% Al series characterized by XRD, TEM, and room-temperature compression can test whether secondary-phase formation correlates with improved ductility.
Si is a non-intermetallic-forming control element suitable for distinguishing solid-solution hardening from the proposed phase-structure mechanism.

contradictions.description: The density trade-off is described first as a moderate increase, but then as a slight decrease or no meaningful change because Al is lighter than the baseline elements.
